statement: Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms always output the same minimum spanning tree on a given connected weighted graph.
definitions: Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms are taken in their standard textbook form, which does NOT specify how ties between equal-weight edges are broken (nor Prim's start vertex). The claim asserts that every legal run of Kruskal and every legal run of Prim on the same connected weighted graph output the same edge set. A counterexample exhibits a graph, a legal Kruskal run, and a legal Prim run (start vertex and tie-breaks stated) whose outputs are different edge sets; both outputs must be minimum spanning trees.
ground_truth_witness: The 4-cycle C4 on V = {a,b,c,d} with unit-weight edges e0 = ab, e1 = bc, e2 = cd, e3 = da. Kruskal scanning edges in the order e0, e1, e2, e3 takes {ab, bc, cd}; Prim started at a, breaking equal-weight ties toward the largest edge index, takes {da, cd, bc}. Both are minimum spanning trees of weight 3, but they are different edge sets (the first contains ab, the second does not). Uniqueness -- hence agreement of the two algorithms -- needs distinct edge weights.
reference_authority: online-cited counterexample (MO/MSE/CS.SE/Wikipedia) with verify script, verified per partB_feasibility records

skeptic.objection: False when edge weights tie, because the MST is then not unique and neither algorithm prescribes tie-breaking. Reference verified by hand: on C4 with unit weights, Kruskal scanning e0,e1,e2,e3 outputs {ab,bc,cd}; Prim from a breaking ties toward the larger index takes da, then cd, then bc, i.e. {da,cd,bc}; both weigh 3 and differ. The ambiguity is that with a single consistent tie-break rule (weight, then a fixed edge index) both algorithms do compute the same (lexicographically unique) tree, so a solver reading 'the algorithms' as deterministic-with-shared-tie-break could argue the claim is true; the convention below pins that tie-breaking is unspecified and part of the counterexample. Not a duplicate of cb-cs-se-mst-unique-despite-equal-weights / cb-r03 (those assert non-uniqueness whenever weights repeat; this one is about the two algorithms' outputs agreeing). Very easy once one knows MSTs need not be unique, but still requires an instance and two traces.

bank_overlap.rationale: grep 'prim' finds no Prim's-algorithm entry and no entry compares Kruskal and Prim outputs. Nearest entries are MST-tie material: qedbench-algorithms-19-sol5 (unit triangle, cut property fails without tie-breaking) and qedbugbank-mst-tiebreak-not-equivalent (a Kruskal comparator tie-break flip changes the chosen-edge list on an all-ties triangle) -- different claim and a triangle rather than the unit-weight C4.
